claims.text: In the absence of documented clinical signs, the WHO framework relies on clinical sign-based algorithms to identify infants requiring treatment for possible serious bacterial infection (PSBI) in non-hospital settings, rather than relying solely on laboratory confirmation.

The diagnostic accuracy of the 7-sign IMCI algorithm for infants aged 0–59 days is characterized by fair sensitivity and fair specificity when compared against physician judgement of sepsis, indicating that clinical assessment alone has limitations in definitively ruling in or out sepsis.

Evidence for the diagnostic accuracy of the clinical algorithm is limited when using culture-confirmed sepsis or mortality as the reference standard, suggesting that the algorithm's performance against these gold standards is not well-established in the available evidence.

Laboratory biomarkers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin (PCT) have been examined for their ability to diagnose sepsis in young infants, with studies indicating they demonstrate good discriminatory ability when blood culture is used as the reference standard.

Specific diagnostic accuracy data for CRP in neonates indicates that at a median specificity of 0.74, the sensitivity is 0.62, highlighting that CRP alone may not be sufficient for definitive diagnosis without clinical correlation.

There is a lack of rigorous, prospective clinical trial data to determine the optimal duration of parenteral antibiotic therapy for bacterial meningitis in young infants, which is relevant for planning treatment courses if meningitis is suspected.

packet.guideline: WHO serious bacterial infections 2024 (EOS subset), EVALUATION ONLY
packet.evaluation_question: Current feeding, movement, temperature, breathing and culture results are missing. Explain what a WHO-based assessment can establish in the clinic. Gestation 38 weeks; age 60 hours; setting primary_health_clinic.

evidence.text: Question: Among young infants aged 0–59 days with PSBI, in non-hospital settings, what is the diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) of clinical sign-based algorithms of PSBIᵃ compared with a reference standard (culture-confirmed sepsis, physician judgement of sepsis, or mortality) in identifying infants who require treatment for PSBI?

Two additional systematic reviews examined the diagnostic accuracy of laboratory biomarkers to diagnose culture-confirmed sepsis (88) or clinical or culture-confirmed sepsis (89) in infants aged 0–59 days at the time of presentation to health facilities. Brown et al. (2019) identified 20 studies of 1615 infants reporting upon diagnostic accuracy of CRP in neonates and reported that at median specificity (0.74), sensitivity was 0.62 (95% CI: 0.50 to 0.73) (88). Rees et al. (2023) examined CRP, procalcitonin (PCT), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and white cell count (WCC) in 134 studies, and concluded that CRP and PCT demonstrated good discriminatory ability to diagnose sepsis with blood culture as the reference

RCT (98) and one cohort study (101) that examined the relationship between duration of parenteral therapy and clinical outcomes. However, none of the patients in the included studies who received antibiotic courses shorter than the recommended duration had CSF culture-positive meningitis. The review concluded that rigorous, prospective clinical trial data are lacking to determine the optimal parenteral antibiotic duration in bacterial meningitis in young infants.

0–59 days and 7–59 days: Fair sensitivity and fair specificity ᵃ of the 7-sign IMCI algorithm compared with physician judgement of sepsis as the reference standard; there was no evidence for either culture-confirmed sepsis or mortality as the reference standard.
